claims.text: The initial material is a non-equiatomic high-entropy alloy with inherent chemical disorder.
The initial alloy has a low-dimensional structure and exhibits a broad magnetic transition.
Spin-dependent machine-learned interatomic potentials can guide compositional tuning of non-equiatomic HEAs.
First-principles alloy methods can investigate finite-temperature magnetic behavior in a transition-metal HEA.
The cited computational approach accounts for temperature-dependent spin fluctuations in paramagnetic CoCrFeMnNi.
DFT-based methods augmented for disorder can be used to systematically optimize the relative concentrations of magnetic elements.
The simulations can represent both finite temperature and chemical disorder typical of HEAs.
Changes in chemical environment and local lattice distortion modulate local exchange interactions between magnetic atoms.
Composition tuning can tailor the strength and spatial distribution of exchange interactions.
The computational method can accurately simulate the effects of composition on magnetic coupling.
Simulation-guided compositional adjustments will sharpen the magnetic phase transition.
Sharpening the magnetic phase transition will increase the magnetocaloric entropy change.
The tuned alloy will have a sharper magnetic transition than the baseline composition.
The tuned alloy will exhibit an enhanced magnetocaloric effect, measured as increased entropy change during magnetic-field cycling.
The untuned baseline composition has a broader magnetic transition and a lower magnetocaloric response.
The magnitude of enhancement is uncertain because simulation accuracy under strong disorder and low-dimensional constraints has not been experimentally validated.
